newsitem.title: CANADA: Japanese imports seen key to Canadian pork prices.
newsitem.headline: Japanese imports seen key to Canadian pork prices.

text.p: Slower Japanese buying of Canadian pork will play a large part in lowering Canadian hog and pork prices in 1997, Jim Morris, president of Canada Pork International (CPI), said.

Morris, in remarks to the Canadian Wheat Board's annual Grain World conference, said Japan's placement of "super safeguard" ad valorem duties on pork imports under world trade rules from July 1996 and January 1996 was extended on February 28 to July, 1997, which will weigh on demand.
Japan's total pork imports rose 12.5 percent in 1996 to 653,178 tonnes, with Canada's share 6.2 percent, Morris said.

"I expect a continuation of soft buying until May, a mad scramble for product until July 1, and then another last half of little Japanese interest. This is not constructive to last half hog prices," Morris said.
Morris said he expects the average Canadian hog price for 1997 to be C$1.60 kg, with hogs peaking in June or July at $1.85.
"April-June Japanese buying will provide the June hog price peak, but it will be short lived," Morris said. "It may well be we have already seen the high prices for the year."
Morris said pork producers were dizzy from 1996's success.
"Many in the industry are money drunk with the success of 1996 and have forgotten that markets can go down," he said.

Last year, hog prices were near record highs most of the year, with much of the gain fueled by Japan's buying ahead of the anticipated July 1 duty. Saskatchewan hog prices averaged C$1.78 per kg, matching the record and a 10-year high.
"Japanese buyers adjusted their patterns, doubling purchases in April-June. They bought 12 months worth of pork in three months," Morris said.
Canadian pork exports in 1996 set a record at 352,688 tonnes, up 14 percent in value terms at C$1.105 billion and up 3.3 percent in tonnage, Morris said.
With live hog exports added in, total Canadian pork exports came to $1.4 billion.
Morris said Canada needs to watch Taiwan's "submarine" pork shipments to Japan as a danger to market share.
"Taiwan will continue to evade the Japanse duty system through false invoicing, and the Japanese government will continue to pretend that it doesn't exist," Morris said.
Aside from slower Japanese buying, Canadian prices will also be pressured by growth in 1997 hog production in the United States due to lower corn prices, Morris said.
EU export subsidies to Russia and other Canadian markets will also be a problem. Steady packer consolidation will also weigh on producer prices, Morris said.
Possible bullish factors, he added, included problems with the Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome disease in the U.S., which "appears to be more virulent this year," Morris said.
Morris also cited Dutch loss of exports due to an outbreak of hog cholera. Trade liberalization pacts with South Korea and China were also expected to be signed in 1997.

Morris said CPI, a producer-packer joint venture aimed at expanding exports, estimated that Canada's pork industry was now 35 percent export-dependent, a figure which could grow to 50 percent "if we can get the industry to grow."

"The bright spot in the entire industry is the growth of the export side. Canada is now the third largest pork exporter in the world and we are really only hemmed in by a lack of supply," Morris said.
(Winnipeg bureau, 204 947 3548)
